title: Listening to Your Favorite Music May Help Ease Pain
paragraphs: Many people do not enjoy having a needle put into their arm at the hospital. However, a new study from Switzerland suggests that listening to your favorite music during the procedure may help to reduce the pain.

The study was carried out by researchers at University Hospital Zurich and published in the journal Frontiers in Pain Research in 2026. It involved 204 adults aged between 17 and 83, who needed to have a small needle inserted into a vein before having an MRI scan.

The participants were divided into four groups. One group listened to their own favorite music, another listened to a piece by Mozart, and a third listened to relaxation music. The fourth group did not listen to any music. The participants listened to the music during the procedure and for two minutes afterward. They then rated their pain immediately after the needle was inserted, as well as 30 seconds and two minutes later.

The researchers found that people who listened to their favorite music reported significantly less pain than those who did not listen to any music, both 30 seconds and two minutes after the procedure. The group that listened to Mozart showed a tendency toward lower pain scores after two minutes, but the difference was not significant. Meanwhile, relaxation music had no clear effect.

The researchers suggest that relaxation music may have been too quiet and repetitive to hold people's attention. In contrast, favorite music is familiar and easy to follow, which may help to distract people and trigger emotional responses that reduce pain.

However, the study had several limitations. The participants were not randomly assigned to the groups, and the pain caused by the small needle was mild, so the results may not apply to more painful procedures. The pain was also only measured for two minutes.

Nevertheless, the researchers believe that favorite music could be a simple, drug-free way to help patients during minor painful procedures. They have called for larger studies to confirm the results.
